title: Multi-department Performance Hub

simple.tagline: Seven areas of the club, one single athlete file.
simple.summary: Physiology, medicine, physiotherapy, psychology, nutrition, social work and education each tracked assessments in their own spreadsheet. Nobody could see an athlete's full file, and the coaching staff had no single consolidated report. I built a dashboard where each area keeps logging things its own way, but everything comes together into one file — and it generates a PDF report per athlete. It's used daily, validated with hundreds of real athletes.

problem: The youth academy's health & performance departments (physiology, medicine, physiotherapy, psychology, nutrition, social work, pedagogy) kept evaluations in separate spreadsheets — no unified per-athlete view, no consolidated report for staff.
targetUser: Academy multidisciplinary staff; two access profiles (regular and admin).
myRole: Sole developer, from import pipeline to deploy.
process: Designed a monolithic Streamlit app with SQLite synced via Google Drive (the database never enters git) and a per-department parser pipeline, runnable locally or through an import page. Iterated the visuals in short feedback cycles with the real user. Rebuilt the per-athlete PDF engine with react-pdf (Node invoked via Python subprocess) after discarding a first approach that failed visual validation.
keyDecisions: Streamlit Community Cloud + SQLite on Drive: zero-cost production.
bcrypt auth + login rate limiting (sliding window per IP), with storage isolated from the main database — which the sync overwrites.
Full dark theme with an accessibility rule: status color is never text color — icon or badge/pill background only.
Wellness only charts on days with a real GPS session for that athlete — eliminates context-free points.
86 pytest cases covering parsers, rate limiting and the PDF bridge.
result: In production and daily use: per-department dashboards, self-service imports, per-athlete PDF validated against hundreds of real athletes, two-step-confirmed backup and restore.
learned: Three production lessons that became rules: an automated test pipeline approved a visually broken PDF — visually validating the real artifact is non-negotiable; an unanchored .gitignore pattern corrupted vendored packages only in deploy — a clean-clone check became mandatory before every push; and tab components that hide panels with display:none permanently zero the height of iframe-based charts — I replaced tabs with radio buttons.
